e.etymology: The Spanish and Portuguese feminine of Jacinto, from Greek Hyakinthos, the name of the hyacinth flower. Saint Jacinta Marto was one of the three children of the 1917 Fatima apparitions.
namesakes: Saint Jacinta Marto (child visionary of Fatima)

e.etymology: A modern American coinage that extends Trevon, itself built on Trevor or Trey with an -on ending, in the pattern of Davion and Javion.

An English surname from several towns called Wellington; the ending is Old English tun, estate, and the first part is uncertain. It became a first name in honor of the Duke of Wellington, victor at Waterloo, and is common in Brazil.

assoc.t: Duke of Wellington, who beat Napoleon at Waterloo
beef Wellington, beef baked in pastry
Wellington boots, rubber rain boots called wellies

e.etymology: A spelling of Citlali, from Nahuatl citlalin, star. The name is widely used in Mexico and in Mexican American families.
A spelling of Brynn, from Welsh bryn, hill. In Wales Bryn is a man's name; the use for girls and the -nn and -nne spellings are American.
From the Scottish and northern English surname Bryden or Brydon, of unclear origin. As a first name it rose with Brayden, Bryson and Bryce in the 2000s.
From Old Norse Erlingr, son or descendant of a jarl, the Norse chieftain's title related to English earl. It came to the US with Scandinavian immigrants.
From Arabic ziyad, increase or abundance, from a verb meaning to grow or add. It is a given name and surname across the Arab world.
The English word spirit, from Latin spiritus, breath, used as a modern word name.

assoc.t: wild mustang of DreamWorks' Spirit films and series

e.etymology: From Arabic faydan, an overflowing, related to fayd, grace or favor. It came into Urdu through Persian and is most common in Pakistan and India.
A spelling of Eleanor used in Scandinavia and now and then in English. Eleanor comes from Old French and Occitan Alienor, the name of Eleanor of Aquitaine; its ultimate meaning is uncertain.

From Arabic Hashim, crusher or breaker, the byname of the Prophet Muhammad's great-grandfather, said to have broken bread for pilgrims in Mecca. The Hashemite dynasty of Jordan takes its name from him.
e.note: In Hebrew, HaShem (the Name) is how observant Jews refer to God.

e.etymology: A recent American coinage in the sound family of Leilani, Kalani and Laylani. It has no recorded history as a traditional name.
A French name, possibly from Azalais, the Occitan form of Adelaide. Saint Marie-Azelie Guerin, known as Zelie Martin, was the mother of Saint Therese of Lisieux and was canonized in 2015.
A modern American name built on oak with the -lan ending of Declan and Rylan, close to the place name Oakland and to Oaklyn.
The name of a legendary king of Phrygia who, in Greek myth, was granted the wish that everything he touched turn to gold. The name is Phrygian and its meaning is unknown.

assoc.t: mythical king whose touch turned everything to gold
Midas auto repair and muffler shops

e.note: The Midas touch is a byword for making money, though in the myth the gift proves a curse.

e.etymology: In Yoruba, ase (said ah-SHAY) is the power to make things happen, also spoken like amen. Separately, Ase or Aase is a Scandinavian women's name from Old Norse ass, god, short for names like Astrid.
A respelling of Kehlani, the name made familiar by R&B singer Kehlani. It is a form of Hawaiian names such as Kailani and Kalani, built on lani, sky or heaven.
A pet form of Tamara, from Hebrew Tamar, palm tree, or of Tamsin, a feminine of Thomas, twin. It boomed after the 1957 film Tammy and the Bachelor and its hit song Tammy.
namesakes: Tammy Wynette (country singer of Stand by Your Man)

e.etymology: From Latin Felicia, literally happy things, from felix, happy or lucky. It is the feminine counterpart of Felix and has been used in England since the Middle Ages.
namesakes: Felicia Day (actress and web series creator)

assoc.t: Bye, Felicia, a dismissive catchphrase from the film Friday

e.note: Bye, Felicia, a line from the 1995 film Friday, became a common brush-off phrase in the 2010s.

e.etymology: A Scandinavian-style spelling of Christopher, from Greek Christophoros, bearing Christ. Legend makes Saint Christopher a giant who carried the Christ child across a river.
The Italian form of Leo, from Latin leo, lion. In the early 1900s Leone was mostly an American girls' name, a feminine of Leon; today it is given mainly to boys.
namesakes: Sergio Leone (director of The Good, the Bad and the Ugly)

e.etymology: The Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Philomena, from Greek Philomene, read as friend of strength or as loved one. Devotion to Saint Philomena spread it in the 1800s, and Italian immigrants brought it to the US.
A spelling of Alicia with an initial E, close also to Elisa and Felicia. Alicia is a Latinized form of Alice, from Old French Adelais, a short form of Germanic Adalheid, noble kind.

e.meaning: of the Geats, a Germanic people
e.etymology: A spelling of Jocelyn popular in Spanish-speaking families. Jocelyn began as a Norman man's name, Joscelin, a pet form of Germanic names built on Gaut, the name of the Geat or Goth people.
A modern coinage that joins the Jay sound to the -lene ending of Marlene and Darlene, a spelling of Jaylene. It has been used mostly in Hispanic families since the 1990s.
A modern American blend of Jade, the green gemstone, with the -lyn ending of Jocelyn and Madelyn.
Mary and Grace written as one name, a pairing with Catholic roots that echoes the Hail Mary's full of grace. Mary is the English form of Hebrew Miriam; Grace is from Latin gratia.

A given name used mainly in Central America and Mexico, also spelled Neri. It is traced either to devotion to Saint Philip Neri, whose surname is Italian, or to the Biblical name Neri, from Hebrew ner, lamp.
The Russian, Czech and Bulgarian form of Paul, from the Latin family name Paulus, small. It reached the Slavic languages through Greek and Church Slavonic with the veneration of the apostle Paul.
namesakes: Pavel Chekov (navigator of the Enterprise in Star Trek)
Pavel Bure (Hall of Fame hockey winger)

e.etymology: Used mainly in Spanish-speaking families, alongside the spelling Dayra. Its source is not settled; name books link it to Daeira, a sea nymph of Greek myth whose name means the knowing one.
The Polish form of Angela, from Latin angelus and Greek angelos, messenger or angel. It became popular in Poland in the 1700s.
